note: Editorial copy based on original archive narratives. No invented awards or campaign metrics.

case_studies.title: #JagaSehatmu bersama KlikDokter
case_studies.hook: Health is what makes everything else possible.
case_studies.deck: A film manifesto that reframes preventive care as a way to enjoy life, rather than another thing to worry about.
parts: The problem with talking about health

Most health messages begin with what might go wrong. The warning signs, the risks, the things people should stop doing. For a brand trying to make preventive care part of everyday life, that familiar language can create distance instead of connection.
A more human starting point

I approached the script from the other end of the conversation. Good health is not simply the absence of illness. It is what lets us show up for the people we love, pursue an ambition, and enjoy the small moments that make an ordinary day worthwhile. The manifesto places those possibilities at the centre of the story.
The line that holds it together

#JagaSehatmu means “Take care of your health.” It is deliberately simple, more like a reassuring reminder than an instruction from a doctor. The film gives that everyday phrase an emotional reason to matter.

case_studies.title: Dicuekin Nana Mirdad, Para Penyakit Curhat
case_studies.hook: What if sickness was the one feeling rejected?
case_studies.deck: A health campaign told from the least expected point of view: diseases complaining that nobody wants them around.
parts: Flip the usual health advertisement

People are used to hearing from doctors, parents, and concerned narrators about the importance of staying healthy. We wanted to make the same point without another stern lecture. So the script gives the microphone to the supposed villains.
The support group nobody asked for

In the film, personified illnesses gather in a therapy-style circle to discuss their shared frustration. Nana Mirdad and her family have been taking better care of themselves, and the diseases are suddenly having a very bad time. The comedy lives in how seriously these ridiculous characters take their own problems.
Humour with a purpose

The joke delivers the campaign message by inversion. Rather than showing people suffering from sickness, we imagine sickness struggling to get their attention. It gives #JagaSehatmu, or “Take care of your health,” a lighter, more memorable voice without turning the message into medical jargon.

case_studies.title: Maxicorn Product Launch
case_studies.hook: Made for people who never play it safe.
case_studies.deck: A bold product introduction shaped around the pace, language, and adrenaline of gaming culture.
parts: Meet the Hyperlifers

The audience insight was about a particular kind of energy. Young people who look for their next challenge, enjoy the thrill of taking risks, and know that good instincts matter as much as bold moves. We called them Hyperlifers.
Make the snack belong in their world

Instead of describing flavour in isolation, I built the launch narrative around the intensity of PUBG Mobile culture. Action, strategy, and a little competitive bravado gave Maxicorn a world to enter. The product's punchy personality could then feel native to the story, not pasted on at the end.
A launch with attitude
The writing keeps the tempo high and the language direct. It is about making an introduction that feels closer to entertainment than a standard product announcement.

case_studies.title: KlikDokter Digital Advertising
case_studies.hook: Good advice still has to earn a second of attention.
case_studies.deck: Turning everyday health information into platform-native copy that people can understand at a glance.
parts: An unforgiving canvas

A banner or social ad rarely has the luxury of a slow build. The reader is scrolling, the space is tight, and the message is competing with everything else in the feed. Health advice has an additional challenge: it can sound either too technical or too preachy.
A different rhythm for each format

Across Google Display Network placements, Facebook, and Instagram, I worked with concise, conversational writing built around recognisable daily concerns. The goal was to make the advice feel immediately relevant, with a helpful nudge rather than a lecture.
Small copy, considered decisions

Every headline, visual cue, and call to action has to carry its weight. This selection shows the quieter craft of copywriting: choosing what to say, what to leave out, and how to make the next step feel easy.

case_studies.title: Ketahui Siapa Sebelum Sapa
case_studies.hook: The most convincing scam calls know exactly which nerve to hit.
case_studies.deck: A personal family scare became the starting point for a humorous film about checking who's calling.
parts: An uncomfortable true starting point

Someone once tried to scam my parents by claiming I had been in an accident. The story was designed to bypass common sense with panic. That experience stayed with me because the tactic was so recognisable: when family is involved, the instinct to act often arrives before the instinct to question.
Find the human story inside the product

For Getcontact's Indonesian launch pitch, I wrote a script grounded in that emotional reflex. Instead of explaining the technology feature by feature, the film dramatizes a situation that could happen to almost anyone. Humour helps turn an unsettling premise into something people can watch and remember.
A warning that works as a line

#KetahuiSiapaSebelumSapa translates to “Know who it is before saying hello.” The phrase folds a useful behaviour into everyday Indonesian speech. It gives the film its resolution and the brand a clear role in the story.
case_studies.role: Original concept and digital film script

case_studies.title: #MaafIbuDiHidupku
case_studies.hook: Some of the most important words are the ones we keep putting off.
case_studies.deck: A Ramadan film about mothers, distance, and the gratitude that rarely makes it into everyday conversation.
parts: The emotional reality of the moment

The campaign was developed around Ramadan during the pandemic, when families were finding new ways to stay close while physically apart. In Indonesia, the season is associated with reflection, reconnection, and asking forgiveness. That made the idea of an unspoken apology especially resonant.
Write for the things people struggle to say

I wanted the script to acknowledge a familiar truth: a mother's care is often constant, but our gratitude is not always expressed. Rather than relying on grand declarations, the narrative leans on small recognisable moments and the emotional weight of distance.
A hashtag with a personal voice
#MaafIbuDiHidupku can be understood as “Mom, I'm sorry for the times I've hurt you.” In the context of Ramadan, the line functions less like a slogan and more like an invitation to reconnect.

case_studies.title: Little Monster
case_studies.hook: When an everyday parenting problem meets a very Indonesian ghost story.
case_studies.deck: A playful folklore-inspired campaign that turns diaper-change reminders into something a little more unforgettable.
parts: A belief hiding in plain sight

In many Indonesian homes, an unusually fussy baby can inspire theories that go well beyond the practical. Folk stories about unseen creatures are familiar cultural shorthand. We saw an opportunity to borrow that language, then reveal a far more ordinary culprit: discomfort from a diaper that needs changing.
Let the monsters do the talking

The creative idea treats those imagined creatures as an entertaining misdirection. The tone borrows from horror, but the purpose is rooted in a real parenting routine. It creates room for comedy, a memorable reveal, and a product message that doesn't have to shout.
A line that completes the joke

I helped shape the concept and wrote #GantiSebelumMenghantui, or “Change it before it comes back to haunt you.” The Indonesian wording connects the act of changing a diaper with the language of ghost stories. That wordplay is what makes the campaign feel local rather than simply translated.

case_studies.title: 1 Detik
case_studies.hook: The smallest songs can be the hardest to get out of your head.
case_studies.deck: A playful product jingle designed for children, with a clear benefit message for the parents listening alongside them.
parts: The two audiences in the room

Writing for a baby-care brand means speaking to parents without forgetting who else hears the message. A jingle has to be fun enough for children to enjoy and useful enough for adults to understand. Neither side should feel like an afterthought.
Make the benefit sing

This was my first jingle project. I leaned into the instantly familiar rhythm of children's entertainment, keeping the language simple, repetitive, and easy to follow. The trick was weaving in product information without turning the lyrics into a spoken brochure.
Designed to be remembered
A good jingle earns another listen through rhythm and playfulness. Here, the copy is not just what is said. It is also the timing, the repetition, and how effortlessly the message can be sung back.

case_studies.title: BCA Finhacks 2019
case_studies.hook: How do you make blockchain less intimidating? Start with a joke.
case_studies.deck: A comedy-led film that brings an abstract technology topic closer to an everyday audience.
parts: Start with the audience, not the technology

Blockchain was the subject, but a detailed technical explanation was never going to be the most entertaining invitation to BCA Finhacks. The creative challenge was to spark curiosity among people who might hear the word and immediately switch off.
Make the unfamiliar feel familiar

I wrote a comedic storyline around the disconnect between a complicated tech term and an accessible, pop-culture-friendly situation featuring Dinda Kirana. The humour does the first bit of work. Once the audience is paying attention, the subject feels less distant.
Clarity is a creative choice
The script isn't trying to deliver a crash course in distributed ledgers. It opens a door. For an event built around new ideas, the writing needed to make curiosity feel easier than intimidation.

case_studies.title: Be Resilient!
case_studies.hook: We cannot prepare children for every future. We can help them face it.
case_studies.deck: A manifesto about raising resilient children in a world that rarely comes with guarantees.
parts: The parenting question behind the brief
Every parent hopes to keep their child safe. But a future full of uncertainty also asks for something beyond protection: the confidence and resilience to respond when things do not go as planned.
From worry to possibility

Writing this manifesto felt personal to me as a father. I wanted the film to speak to parents with empathy, not anxiety. The narrative shifts attention from what the future might throw at children to the inner strength they can develop with encouragement and care.
A brand voice that feels supportive
The language is optimistic without promising an easy future. It positions Nutriclub as a companion to parents who want to nurture curiosity, confidence, and resilience, one ordinary day at a time.

case_studies.title: Berani Matahari
case_studies.hook: Sunscreen advice works better when it sounds like a friend.
case_studies.deck: A series of light, conversational films that meet Indonesian skincare habits with humour rather than a lecture.
parts: A familiar barrier

For many young people, sun protection can feel like an extra step rather than an essential part of a routine. The brief called for a way to make the subject more approachable without flattening it into generic skincare advice.
Find the comedy in real habits

I wrote around the little rationalisations people make, including the assumption that a cloudy day is a reason to skip sunscreen. Familiar behaviours gave the scripts both their humour and their usefulness. The characters sound like people talking to one another, not experts reading instructions.
A little wit, a practical takeaway

Berani Matahari means “Brave enough for the sun.” The series brings confidence, warmth, and playful dialogue to a functional message. Each short film aims to entertain first, then leave the viewer with a reason to think differently about daily protection.

case_studies.title: Sambal Indofood Social
case_studies.hook: If the internet has a personality, a sambal brand can have one too.
case_studies.deck: Giving an everyday condiment a sharper, more culturally fluent voice in social feeds.
parts: The product was already familiar

Sambal is part of everyday food culture in Indonesia. The challenge was not to introduce people to chilli sauce. It was to make a familiar household brand feel naturally present in the conversations younger audiences were having online.
Write for the feed, not the boardroom

The content takes cues from memes, local slang, playful exchanges, and pop-culture references. I developed a voice that could be quick, cheeky, and recognisably Indonesian. The brand behaves more like someone joining the conversation than a product interrupting it.
Consistency without repetition
A social voice has to stretch across many posts without losing its character. The work explores how to keep the humour fresh while making the brand feel at home in the daily scroll.

case_studies.title: Think Outside the Paper
case_studies.hook: An ordinary material can carry an extraordinary idea.
case_studies.deck: Building a single brand thought that could live across a manifesto, print advertising, and a corporate website.
parts: Find a philosophy bigger than a product

BMJ operates in a highly specialised paper and packaging category. The writing challenge was to express the company's point of view in a way that went beyond specifications, materials, and manufacturing processes.
A familiar phrase, rewritten for the brand

I developed Think Outside the Paper as the organising idea. It borrows the invitation of “think outside the box,” then makes paper itself the creative starting point. The line suggests imagination and possibility in a category often discussed in purely functional terms.
One thought, several expressions

From the manifesto to a print series built around imagination and the language of the corporate site, the same thought needed to stay consistent while taking different shapes. This is the kind of copywriting I enjoy: establishing a voice that remains recognisable across very different formats.
case_studies.role: Brand line, manifesto, print and corporate copywriting

case_studies.title: #UnboxingCaleg
case_studies.hook: Before you choose a candidate, shouldn't you know what's inside the box?
case_studies.deck: Borrowing the language of online unboxing to make legislative candidates easier for young voters to discover.
parts: A serious question with a simple obstacle

Indonesian legislative elections ask voters to make decisions about a long list of candidates. For younger audiences, even knowing where to begin can be difficult. The project sought to make candidate information more approachable without telling anyone who to vote for.
Turn the internet's format into the idea

The creative leap was to borrow the familiar format of an unboxing video. Instead of unpacking a product, #UnboxingCaleg invites people to unpack the backgrounds and platforms of caleg, the Indonesian shorthand for legislative candidates. It makes political research feel closer to a recognisable online habit.
Build a language people will open

I worked on the narrative and social content, including witty teasers and short comedic pieces that encouraged people to explore the candidate reviews. The purpose was not to make politics trivial. It was to reduce the friction of paying attention. Better information starts with getting people interested enough to look.
case_studies.role: Campaign narrative, social copywriting and content
